newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium's year of living in shame.
newsitem.headline: Belgium's year of living in shame.

text.p: One year ago the discovery of two sexually abused and murdered young girls plunged Belgians into shock, shame, international humiliation, mutual recrimination, and self analysis.
The shock remains, but the outpouring of anger that prompted a rash of public demonstrations has given way to a sort of resigned phlegmatism.

A recent opinion poll in La Derniere Heure newspaper showed nearly 90 percent of people thought the full story would never be known, and nearly 70 percent believed that no fundamental changes would result from the tragedy.

The discovery of eight-year-olds Julie Lejeune and Melissa Russo in a shallow grave in the garden of an unremarkable house in the sleepy town of Sars-La-Buissiere on August 17, 1996 began a trail of revelations that shook Belgium to its roots.

Two weeks later child rapist Marc Dutroux, who led police to Julie and Melissa after he was arrested for the abduction and abuse of two other young girls, showed investigators where teenagers An Marchal and Eefje Lambrecks lay buried.
Dutroux has been charged with the murder of all four, but is unlikely to come to trial for at least another year.

Newspapers began revealing details of the bungled police investigations into the original disappearances and of the apparent indifference and regional rivalries of magistrates originally in charge of the cases.
How, the public asked, had a man who was still on parole after being released early from a 13-year sentence for multiple child rape, escaped police attention for so long.

One theory that became common currency, and which is still being investigated by an all-party parliamentary committee, was that Dutroux and his accomplices -- including his second wife Michelle Martin -- had friends in high places.
The public anger erupted onto the streets of Brussels on October 20 when more than 250,000 people marched to demonstrate their disgust at a system seen as deeply rotten.
VAST DEMONSTRATION FORCED GOVERNMENT ACTION
It was the biggest ever peacetime demonstration in Belgium and one that finally catapulted the government into action.
Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene promised a raft of changes in the police and judicial system, and the parliamentary enquiry into the investigations was set up.
Many of these changes are now working slowly through the machinery of government.

The decision to parole a sex offender will no longer lie with the justice minister, a centre for missing children is being set up, an investigating magistrate will be appointed when a child goes missing and the parents will be kept informed.
But reform of the police and of the magistrature -- both cited as crucial in the preliminary report presented in April by the parliamentary commission -- are making slow progress.

The trouble, says Chris Eliaerts, professor of criminology at Brussels Free University, lies in both the political nature of magistrates' appointments and the language divisions between Belgium's French speaking south and Dutch speaking north.

"This is a very complex country. The language divisions, the local party power bases, the coalition government. So it is difficult to get a consensus on anything let alone complex structures such as these," he told Reuters.
The parliamentary commission recommended merging the country's three police forces -- the communal police, judicial police and gendarmes -- into one supra-national body.
Lack of communication between these forces was a key failure cited in the committee's April report.
The police forces themselves oppose the plan, so do local mayors and even deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt, forcing Dehaene to intercede.
Reform of the magistrature has proved an even thornier issue, involving as it does the exercise of political influence.
"The political and business say in the appointment of magistrates is a big problem, and changing it will be difficult," Eliaerts said.
"Controlling the quality of magistrates...and the fact that they are appointed for life, is also a problem. Simply, there are too many people who are in the wrong place.
"These are very important changes. They will come, but they will take time," he added. "I was pessimistic in the beginning, but now I am not so much.
"The Dutroux case was a very important moment in our history. It will have an effect for years to come."
His optimism, however, is far from universal.

Marc Verwilgen, the head of the parliamentary committee which is due to produce its report on a possible cover-up for Dutroux and his gang at the end of September, has complained that his work is being ridiculed.

The minority opposition green parties in the Belgian parliament have tabled a motion calling on the four-party coalition government to resign, citing its failure to carry through its promises of reform.
The motion, motivated as much by a genuine anger as by political design, is bound to fail.

But it will embarrass a government already surrounded by bribery scandals and facing accusations that it has abandoned all else in its single-minded focus on qualifying for the European Union's single currency.

There is also a feeling that the human tragedy of the murders of Julie, Melissa, An and Eefje, as well as of Loubna Benaissa -- whose body was discovered in February this year -- has in some way been tainted by politics.
National elections are not due until the end of 1999, but there is a widely held view that they may be held as early as the middle of next year.
La Derniere Heure summed up the national mood. Nearly 86 percent of the 2,000 people questioned said there was no point in taking part in another national demonstration.
